extracted.intended_audience: appellate attorneys, trial lawyers, and litigants (including pro se) handling Alaska construction-defect/tort appeals and related civil procedure issues
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria governing appeals in Alaska construction-defect and related tort/contract cases (statute of limitations, evidentiary admissibility, negligence elements, relief from judgment, remedies, and constitutionality of process). Useful for preparing/appraising appellate briefs and court rulings in such matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alaska statutory time limits for construction-defect actions (AS 09.18.8055)
rubrics_metrics.description: "(a) No action ... to recover damages ... for a deficiency in the design, planning, supervision or observation of construction or construction of an improvement to real property ... may be brought against a person ... more than six years after substantial completion of an improvement." (text of AS 69.18.8055 as quoted on the page)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute provides the baseline limitations: generally six years from substantial completion; subsection (b) permits an action for injury occurring during the sixth year to be brought within two years after the injury, but in no event more than eight years after substantial completion. Subsection (d) excludes asserting the limitation as a defense where a person is in actual possession or control of the improvement at the time the deficiency constitutes the proximate cause of the injury. The brief emphasizes that applying or ignoring this statute determines whether a non-resident was unfairly subjected to suit after the limitations period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of negligence claim for construction-defect (jury instruction standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover on negligence the plaintiffs must prove by a preponderance of the evidence (a) that the defendant was negligent, (b) that the defendant's negligence was a legal cause (proximate cause) of the plaintiffs' harm, and (c) that the plaintiffs suffered damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superior court instructed the jury defining negligence and proximate cause; the jury's special verdicts finding negligence and causation support judgment. Appellate review may affirm on the independent negligence basis even if other theories (agency, partnership) are contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of evidence — probative value vs unfair prejudice (Alaska Rules 401 & 403)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence is admissible if relevant (Alaska R. Evid. 401) and its probative value is not substantially outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice, confusion or misleading the jury (Alaska R. Evid. 403).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court held admission of prior house plans and the Beaver brochure was within the trial court's discretion because the plans/brochure were relevant to the issues (e.g., design, reliance) and probative value was not outweighed by unfair prejudice. Trial courts' discretionary evidentiary rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for new trial based on newly discovered evidence (Montgomery Ward factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly discovered evidence must (1) probably change the result on a new trial; (2) have been discovered since the trial; (3) be such that it could not have been discovered before trial by due diligence; (4) be material; and (5) not be merely cumulative or impeaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors (from Montgomery Ward v. Thomas, 394 P.2d 774 (Alaska 1964)) guide whether a Rule 59 new-trial or similar motion should be granted. The court applied these standards and found the superior court not clearly mistaken in denying relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief from judgment analysis for "new evidence" under post-judgment rules (Rule 60(b)/68(b) vs Rule 59)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the asserted ground for relief is newly discovered evidence, relief under a post-judgment motion (labeled here as Civil Rule 68(b) motions for relief from judgment) is analyzed similarly to a Rule 59 motion for a new trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief and opinion note procedural rules allowing courts to treat relief-from-judgment motions raising new evidence as governed by the same standards applicable to new-trial motions (see Montgomery Ward standard). Precise rule numbers cited in filings may vary, but the substantive analysis is the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception to limitations where defendant is in actual possession or control
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory limitation shall not be asserted by way of defense by a person in actual possession or control, as owner, tenant, or otherwise, of an improvement at the time a deficiency in an improvement constitutes the proximate cause of the injury or death for which it is proposed to bring an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory exception narrows the defense of limitations if the alleged tortfeasor is in control/possession when the deficiency causes injury. The opinion cites subsection (d) as part of AS 69.18.8055.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate affirmation on independent grounds (alternative basis doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellate court may affirm a judgment on an independent basis supported by the record even if other jury findings (agency, partnership, joint venture) are challenged on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here, although Chisum challenged jury findings on agency/partnership, the court concluded that the negligence special verdicts and supporting evidence furnished an independent basis to uphold the judgment against Chisum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for finding agency, joint venture, or partnership (fact-intensive inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings that defendants were agent, joint venturers, or partners may be based on conduct and relationships over time (e.g., shared activities, representations, business dealings) and may support joint and several liability when the jury so finds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury found Riem to be Chisum's agent and that a partnership/joint venture existed; appellants argued insufficient evidence. The opinion reviews the factual record (brochures, mill ownership, representations) and sustains the jury verdicts. Although the court did not list formal elements in one place, it applied standard sufficiency-of-evidence review to these factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate contract remedy principle — rescission vs money judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where plaintiff retains the property and is awarded full monetary recovery, the remedy may be inconsistent; rescission and restitution typically require return of the property, while an award of full contract damages without return may be inappropriate absent findings justifying such relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellant argued that plaintiffs cannot 'keep the house and have it paid for in full' and that if the remedy is rescission, the plaintiffs should return the home. This represents a remedial/legal check ensuring that the form of relief aligns with equitable principles and contract remedy law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for proving reliance and consequences of discovery failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of reliance on promotional materials (e.g., advertising brochures) requires establishing that the plaintiff had and relied on the material at the relevant time; discovery failures that prevent a defendant from obtaining exculpatory evidence (e.g., dates of printing/shipment) can be grounds for post-trial relief if the evidence meets the Montgomery Ward factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case, appellant demonstrated documentary evidence (invoices, air bills) showing brochures were printed/shipped after the loan/contract; failure to produce those documents in discovery prejudiced the defense at trial and formed the basis for motions for a new trial/relief from judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of expert testimony on structural defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony that the plans were structurally defective and that the resulting house was unsafe is highly probative on negligence and causation in construction-defect litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court noted that all but one expert concluded the house was structurally unsound and that experts agreed the plans were deficient; such consensus provided strong evidentiary support for negligence verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional claims regarding statute application — equal protection and due process contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that a state court's failure to apply a statute of limitations to a nonresident amounts to denial of equal protection or deprivation of property without due process requires showing discriminatory application or procedural unfairness violating the Fourteenth Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellant urged that denying enforcement of the statutory limitation against a nonresident denied equal protection and due process. The brief frames such constitutional arguments as grounds for Supreme Court review (certiorari) when state action treats residents and nonresidents differently or ignores statute-based protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal jurisdiction and service-of-process fairness considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Asserting in personam jurisdiction over a defendant who has not resided in the state for many years, who lacks privity with the plaintiff, and whose contacts were limited (mail/telephone), raises due-process concerns about fairness of exercising jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellant argued that service of process nearly seven years after the act, with long absence from the state and no direct dealings with plaintiffs, implicated jurisdictional/due process fairness; courts consider defendant's contacts, notice, and whether asserting jurisdiction comports with constitutional due process.
